text: I found Q3.4 on Absalon data and my sensitive privacy questions difficult because I worry about being constantly monitored while working part-time to support myself financially. In contrast, many participants accept more invasive data if it helps identify struggling peers broadly; this tension between broad surveillance and targeted help is hard for me to resolve without an explicit opt-out mechanism or clear justification that the intervention actually benefits the student first, not just flags them as a risk factor.

I found Q4 explainability and Q7 intervention preferences hardest to weigh together. While I accept moderate data for identification if fairness improves—like using disability info—I find myself hesitating on personalized outreach versus generic emails. In a health scenario, knowing why I'm flagged matters more than broad statistics. However, the group accepted high-level factors better than me because they view it as "risk management," whereas I see it as potential stigma.

The tension lies in balancing protection with inclusion. If we adopt an explicit opt-out for sensitive data and ensure all interventions are voluntary, could we agree on using disability context only to avoid false positives? Perhaps the issue isn't just the model's accuracy but ensuring students feel safe enough to engage with support at all.

I struggled with Q3.4 and sensitive data because I know what it's like to feel monitored just for trying my best. My profile was different; while others emphasized fairness or accuracy thresholds that felt abstract to me personally as a former dropout, the core tension is whether support systems should flag risk before we've even tried again.

The most important design question isn't about data types alone, but ensuring students trust they aren't being punished for struggling. I would accept disability context if it helps avoid false positives for those like me who just need more time than others to demonstrate progress. The group prioritized catching everyone broadly; we might agree that a better approach is protecting the vulnerable first by minimizing invasive data until there's no reasonable doubt.

I found Q3.4 and Q5.2 challenging because they force a trade-off between catching every struggling student versus protecting privacy for specific groups like those with disabilities or from marginalized backgrounds. While many accept high thresholds to maximize identification, I argued earlier that sensitive data should be acceptable only if it improves fairness (Q3.6) but never just increases accuracy, as we risk stigmatizing students who need support less than others based on their background rather than performance.

In contrast to the group's preference for personalized outreach, I believe generic email interventions are more appropriate initially to reduce stigma and preserve trust. The key tension lies in whether our goal should be "maximum help" or "right help without harm." Perhaps a solution outside the model is establishing an explicit opt-out mechanism for sensitive data and ensuring all flagged students receive support that respects their dignity before escalating contact frequency.

I find Q3.6 on fairness particularly important; I answered 'acceptable_regardless' for disability data because it directly impacts my experience of being able to study with ADHD or deadlines. Without this context, the model might wrongly flag me just for taking more time than usual. This feels less like risk and more about understanding barriers. In contrast, the group prioritized catching everyone broadly, often at high thresholds that ignore privacy trade-offs for groups like mine. My main concern is ensuring we don't stigmatize struggling students before trying to help them. Perhaps an opt-out mechanism or a focus on "right help" without false positives would resolve this tension better than just adjusting data accuracy.

I found Q4.1 extremely hard because I cannot imagine advising a student without knowing exactly why they were flagged; "black box" models feel punitive to me personally and my peers alike. While others prioritize catching everyone broadly, we must design systems where explanations are clear before trust erodes. My position differs from those accepting high thresholds for accuracy: explainability is non-negotiable here, not a trade-off variable. If advisors cannot justify the flag without violating student dignity or privacy assumptions, no amount of identification efficiency will make the system acceptable to us in practice.

The tension lies in whether our goal is "maximum help" or "right help without harm." We must design systems where explanations are clear before trust erodes; otherwise, no amount of efficiency will make the system acceptable in practice for students like me.

I found Q3.4 and Q5.2 difficult because I need to know if a model catches people based on patterns or my actual background. While many accept high thresholds for accuracy, I worry that without clear reasons why someone is flagged—like S8 mentioned—it feels punitive rather than supportive. I agreed with A3's point: explainability must be non-negotiable; black-box predictions erode trust before they ever build help-seeking behavior. My answer emphasized a 'small' improvement threshold for less invasive data, balancing the need to catch those who might struggle versus avoiding unnecessary stigma for myself as someone already resilient enough not to drop out easily based on grades alone. We should agree that while broad support is good, it shouldn't come at the cost of making students feel monitored rather than supported.

I struggled with Q3.4 on Absalon data and Q5.2's fairness trade-offs. I answered that online activity data should never be used for me specifically due to feeling surveilled. For fairness regarding first-generation students, I accepted a 'large' improvement threshold to ensure we don't miss those like my peers who lack external safety nets.

The group prioritized broad accuracy and personalized outreach, while I emphasize protecting dignity through generic emails and opt-outs. The tension is between maximizing help for vulnerable groups versus avoiding stigma that silences them further. Perhaps the solution lies outside the model itself: ensuring interventions are never punitive but truly supportive before they erode trust. We must design systems where a flag feels like an invitation to support, not proof of failure.

I found Q3.4 and my sensitive data questions challenging because being flagged just for trying harder feels punitive rather than supportive. While many prioritized catching every struggling student broadly to help more people, I worried about creating self-fulfilling prophecies where students feel monitored before we've even tried again. The group's push for broad accuracy often ignored privacy trade-offs that harm trust with vulnerable groups like myself or first-gen peers. Perhaps the solution isn't just adjusting data thresholds but designing systems where flags imply support, not failure—like opt-outs and voluntary contact methods I prefer (generic emails over personalized outreach). We agreed explainability is non-negotiable for advisors; without clear reasons ("why"), no amount of identification efficiency will make this system acceptable to students in practice.

I struggled with Q3.6 regarding sensitive data for fairness; I answered that some factors like disability should be acceptable regardless of identification gains because missing me is worse than false positives. The group often prioritized broad accuracy over this nuance, which felt risky given my experience as an international student adapting to new systems. My key tension was with those who preferred personalized outreach or higher data thresholds; I believe generic emails and opt-out mechanisms preserve trust better than aggressive monitoring. While explainability is non-negotiable for the university (as others noted), protecting vulnerable students from stigma through minimal, dignified intervention feels more ethical than maximizing help at all costs.

I found Q3.4 on Absalon data particularly difficult; seeing my digital habits flagged felt like surveillance rather than support. While others accepted high thresholds for accuracy or emphasized fairness across groups, I focused heavily on my own experience: without context explaining *why* a flag was raised (Q4), the system feels punitive to someone managing a chronic health condition.

I believe explainability is non-negotiable; it builds trust before we can offer help. The tension lies in balancing broad catch-all strategies with protecting vulnerable students from stigma. A potential solution outside the model itself might be an explicit opt-out mechanism for sensitive data and ensuring all outreach remains voluntary, like generic emails instead of personalized warnings until support has been offered first.
